issues.legal_issue: A town-planning decision is not invalid for failure to communicate reasons in the decision extract when the reasons are included in the published scheme and the affected party can inspect that scheme but does not do so.
material_facts: The affected owner objected to the proposed changes and valuations in a town-planning scheme.
The reasons for the decision were included in the final scheme published by the arbitrator.
The extract sent to the owner stated that the final scheme was available for inspection at the arbitrator’s office.
The owner did not use the opportunity to inspect the final scheme.
issues.conclusion: The decision was not defective in law, and there was no violation of natural justice, because the reasons were available for inspection in the published scheme.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assumed that Section 32 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 impliedly required the Town Planning Officer to give reasons for decisions under that section. It held that, where reasons were included in the final scheme published under Section 28 and the affected party was told that the scheme was available for inspection, failure to include those reasons in the extract sent to that party did not make the decision unlawful when the party did not inspect the scheme. No earlier case was relied on to resolve this issue.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_challenge and reasons_in_published_scheme and inspection_was_available and party_did_not_inspect

predicates.town_planning_scheme_challenge: A party challenged a decision made in preparing or administering a town-planning scheme.
predicates.reasons_in_published_scheme: The decision-maker included the reasons for the decision in the published scheme.
predicates.inspection_was_available: The affected party was informed that the published scheme could be inspected.
predicates.party_did_not_inspect: The affected party did not use the opportunity to inspect the published scheme.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a town-planning decision, reasons included in a published scheme that was available for inspection but not inspected do not make the decision invalid merely because the reasons were absent from the extract sent to the party.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot argue the merits of a valuation decision in a later appeal after its statutory appeal against that decision was rejected as untimely.
material_facts: The owner received an extract of the final scheme containing the valuation decision.
The owner’s appeal to the Board of Appeal was rejected because it was filed beyond the prescribed time.
The Court directed that the owner could not argue the valuation issue in the appeal before it.
issues.conclusion: The owner was not entitled to argue the question of valuation in the appeal before the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 provided a one-month period for appealing specified Town Planning Officer decisions. The Court’s order confined the appeal to arguments that could be urged before the High Court and excluded valuation because the appeal to the Board of Appeal had been filed out of time. No earlier case was relied on to resolve this issue.

predicates.valuation_appeal_proceeding: A party sought to argue the merits of a valuation decision in a later appeal.
predicates.board_appeal_was_untimely: The party’s appeal against the valuation decision to the designated appeal body was rejected as filed beyond the prescribed time.

issues.definition: In a later appeal concerning a valuation decision, an appeal rejected as untimely prevents the party from arguing the valuation issue.
